blocks.text: Chrysostom on Matth., Homil. 12: Ἦλθε τὸ πνεῦμα ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς [Ēlthe to pneuma en eidei peristeras]. Isidore of Pelusium, Epist. 106: Ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς τὸ θεῖον ἐπεφάνη πνεῦμα [En eidei peristeras to theion epephanē pneuma]. Cyril on John: Περιστερᾶς ἐν σχήματι [Peristeras en schēmati]. And: ἐν τῷ τῆς περιστερᾶς σχηματισμῷ [en tō tēs peristeras schēmatismō]. The author of the book On the Wonders of Scripture, under Augustine's name, book 3, ch. 5: “But although the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon the Lord in bodily form, there is not the least doubt that he did not take the dove from among the birds, but from the air.” The author of the book [II, 570] On the Sacraments, under Ambrose's name, book 1, ch. 5: “And behold! the Spirit descended as a dove: not a dove descended, but as it were a dove.” And a little later: “He descended from heaven not in the reality of a dove, but in the appearance of a dove.” Procopius of Gaza on Gen. XVIII: “The Holy Spirit came into our sight in the appearance of a dove; yet it was not a dove, because it did not have the nature that a dove has.” Third, it must be noted that Tertullian errs very gravely. For he says things of the Holy Spirit that cannot be true unless one imagines that the Holy Spirit took a dove to himself in hypostatic union. “The Spirit,” he says, “was as truly a dove as he was Spirit, and he had not destroyed his own substance by assuming a foreign one.” From this another error arose, namely that the Holy Spirit is as far below Christ as a dove is below a man. So Martial, comparing Stella's dove with Catullus's sparrow, maintains that Stella is a better poet than Catullus by as much
As a dove is greater than a sparrow.
